papers.Title: Unbundling Multimodal Vision Encoding
papers.Abstract: How multimodal language models should encode visual input remains up for debate. Most models use a pretrained vision encoder, while some recent recipes train the encoder from scratch with the language model or remove it entirely. Vision encoders bundle together three design choices: a visual prior from upstream pretraining, dedicated vision capacity, and pre-fusion placement of that capacity (i.e., before the multimodal backbone). Because published models also differ in data, architecture, and compute, comparing them cannot isolate the effect of each choice. We disentangle these choices via a controlled framework where we pretrain all models from scratch on common data and compare them on visual question answering and language benchmarks at matched lifetime compute. We find that the visual prior is not necessary; an encoder trained jointly from scratch is on par with a pretrained one, without a separate training stage. What matters instead is dedicated vision capacity: an encoder-free model trails on visual understanding even when its backbone is enlarged by the encoder's parameter count. Yet that capacity need not precede multimodal fusion, as vision-only modules added in-fusion to early backbone layers perform comparably to a pre-fusion encoder and can lower time to first token. These results also hold across backbone sizes, when encoder pretraining is treated as free, and when starting from a pretrained language model. Overall, our findings favor dedicated vision capacity trained jointly with the backbone and placed early within it.
papers.Core_Innovation: Researchers decoupled three encoder design choices—visual prior, dedicated capacity, and pre-fusion placement—by pretraining all models from scratch on identical data. Performance isolation reveals that dedicated vision capacity, not the visual prior, drives multimodal QA and language benchmark results.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Artificial Intelligence, Computer Vision, Generative AI
papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Pretrained Vision Encoders, Legacy Computer Vision Infrastructure
papers.Decision_Perspective: Product teams should immediately prototype multimodal models using from-scratch vision encoders with dedicated capacity allocation, eliminating pretrained prior dependencies. Organizations must phase out licensed vision encoder subscriptions for new deployments within 12 months if compute budgets allow retraining.
papers.Tags: Multimodal AI, Vision Encoding, Model Efficiency, Compute Optimization
papers.Hook: Visual priors unnecessary; from-scratch training matches pretrained encoders with dedicated capacity.

papers.Title: ArchSpace: Recording, Reviewing, and Referencing LLM Architecture Research
papers.Abstract: Model architecture shapes the scaling behavior, training efficiency, and inference cost of LLMs, making it a central focus of both industry and academia. In industry, teams such as those behind DeepSeek, Qwen, and Kimi routinely introduce architectural innovations, yet public reports rarely document which ideas succeeded, which were abandoned, and why. In academia, limited compute and inconsistent baselines often restrict evaluations to small-scale, single-point comparisons, making it difficult to establish whether improvements hold at larger scales or translate into broader impact. ArchSpace addresses both gaps as a public platform for Recording, Reviewing, and Referencing Architecture Researc}: each proposal is recorded with its experiments and reasoning, reviewed by the community, and referenced by later work. To evaluate ideas before costly large-scale training, ArchSpace leverages scaling laws to predict model loss at larger scales from smaller experiments, a practice widely adopted in industry. We provide initial references that make the platform usable: Qwen3.5 and OLMo3 baselines, fitted scaling laws, and a reusable training recipe. Ideas validated through this review can in turn become new baselines, and ArchSpace thereby aims to broaden the range of ideas that shape the next generation of models.
papers.Core_Innovation: ArchSpace records architecture proposals with full experimental metadata and uses scaling laws to predict loss at target compute, enabling architecture comparison without full training.
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate budget to integrate ArchSpace-style architecture recording into internal LLM workflows within the next 90 days. Mandate scaling law validation on all new architecture proposals before full training commitment.
papers.Tags: architecture, scaling laws, platform, evaluation
papers.Hook: Scaling laws now predict LLM loss from small architecture experiments before costly training.

papers.Title: Internalizing Investment Mandates: A Neurosymbolic RL Approach to Portfolio Allocation
papers.Abstract: Institutional portfolios operate under investment policy statements that specify asset allocation constraints, often conditioned on market regime information. Deep reinforcement learning has been shown to optimize financial performance but typically does not enforce rule compliance, making it unsuitable for real-world deployment. Existing neurosymbolic methods such as Probabilistic Logic Policy Gradient (PLPG) offer constraint-satisfying reinforcement learning (RL) via differentiable symbolic supervision but assume a finite, discrete action space. We present a PLPG-inspired continuous allocation method that estimates the probability that the policy's own executed action satisfies the investment mandate, using reparameterized Monte Carlo sampling, and adds it to the training objective. No post-hoc enforcement mechanism intercepts actions at inference time and compliance is learned by the agent. Audited directly on deterministic mean actions with no correction, the policy reduces violations of a six-rule regime-conditional mandate from 96-98% for unconstrained RL and 33.4% for a reward-penalty baseline to 4.8%, showing that a continuous-action neurosymbolic policy can substantially internalize a symbolic mandate.
papers.Core_Innovation: Integrates a differentiable symbolic supervisor into the reward function using reparameterized Monte Carlo sampling to handle continuous action spaces.
papers.Decision_Perspective: Replace rule-based post-trade compliance filters with this integrated RL architecture in Q3. Fund the migration of legacy portfolio optimizers to neurosymbolic frameworks to reduce execution latency.
papers.Tags: Neurosymbolic AI, Reinforcement Learning, Portfolio Optimization, Constraint Satisfaction
papers.Hook: RL agents can now learn to obey complex investment mandates without post-hoc action clipping.

papers.Title: AgentSSL: Can MLE Agents Leverage Unlabeled Data?
papers.Abstract: Applying machine learning systems to new domains introduces bottlenecks in both labeled data acquisition and manual pipeline engineering. While recent MLE agents show promise in automating pipeline design, they have been studied almost exclusively in fully supervised settings, leaving them untested in realistic regimes where labeled data is scarce but unlabeled data is abundant. In this work, we introduce Agentic Semi-Supervised Learning (AgentSSL), framing SSL as a program search problem and studying how agents navigate this space under limited supervision. We find that even under weak feedback and matched compute, agents can synthesize code that combines and adapts established SSL techniques, exceeding the strongest human-engineered baselines in 8 of 12 settings by up to +21.8%. However, our results identify program selection as a critical bottleneck in AgentSSL, where performance drops by as much as 47% when selecting based on the agent's feedback metric. To systematically study this bottleneck, we introduce ProgramSelectBench, a large-scale benchmark with a combined total of 16,977 agent-generated and human-engineered SSL programs, and evaluate both unsupervised and active program selection methods. We further evaluate AgentSSL on real-world ecology detection tasks, highlighting the opportunities and challenges of transferring agent-discovered strategies beyond controlled benchmarks.
papers.Core_Innovation: AgentSSL reframes semi-supervised learning as a program search problem, enabling agents to synthesize and combine SSL code under weak feedback
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate R&D resources to build internal AgentSSL prototypes within 3 quarters, targeting the automation of SSL pipeline design. Direct funding specifically toward resolving the program selection bottleneck that degrades agent performance by up to 47%
papers.Tags: AgentSSL,Semi-Supervised Learning,Program Search,Unlabeled Data
papers.Hook: MLE agents automatically synthesize SSL pipelines from unlabeled data, matching or exceeding human design

papers.Title: CoReMem: Cost-Internalizing Memory for Successive Coding Tasks with Prospective Valuation
papers.Abstract: Coding agents tackle successive tasks on an evolving repository, carrying forward edits and writing memory before the next task is known. Selecting memory for unknown next tasks requires balancing future usefulness against the costs of writing and reading it. The actor must also decide when acting on available memory saves effort as the task unfolds. We introduce Coding-Repository Memory (CoReMem), a cost-internalizing framework that guides memory design and actor adaptation through measured memory value on the next task. Prospective segment valuation compares runs of the next task with and without individual trajectory segments from the same inherited repository state, guiding a compact memory built around anchors: repository locations and executable checks. Actor adaptation estimates on-policy memory value within rollout groups with and without memory, using a reward that prioritizes resolution and penalizes step count in successful runs. Provenance-gated value credit assigns the additional value term to steps identified as using memory-supplied anchors, while every step retains outcome credit. On ChainSWE, CoReMem raises the 27B actor's resolve rate from 21.0% to 25.7%, with 17% fewer steps and 11% fewer total cache-aware tokens, including memory-module calls, relative to the untrained actor model without memory.
papers.Core_Innovation: Prospective segment valuation quantifies memory utility by contrasting task runs with and without inherited segments, directing compact memory toward repository locations and executable checks.
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate funding to prototype CoReMem's prospective valuation in our internal code-assist system within the next two quarters. Halt development of legacy memory-agnostic code-review tools that cannot quantify segment-level task utility.
papers.Tags: CoReMem, Prospective Valuation, Memory Anchors
papers.Hook: Prospective segment valuation enables cost-aware memory selection for successive coding tasks.

papers.Title: Linking Rapid Learning to Compositional Structure in Neural Networks: Evidence from Additive Analogies in Meta-Learned Parameter Spaces
papers.Abstract: Humans can learn rapidly from limited experience, while neural networks typically require extensive training. In this work, we investigate what properties of a neural network can enable it to learn rapidly. We study neural networks that have been optimized via meta-learning, a technique that exposes a network to many related functions to facilitate its subsequent learning of similar functions. Prior work has shown that these meta-learned networks can learn new functions rapidly, but how they do so remains unclear. To investigate their internal structure, we take inspiration from classic work demonstrating additive relationships among the learned vectors that neural networks use to represent words (e.g., "king" minus "man" plus "woman" approximates "queen"). Analogously, we look for additive relationships among a meta-learned network's "representations" of different functions; when a meta-learned network rapidly learns to implement a specific function, all of its adapted parameter values can be concatenated into a single vector that we treat as representing the function. We find that such parameter vectors can be added and subtracted according to symbolic relationships among the functions they represent, yielding new parameter vectors that successfully represent the functions predicted by the corresponding symbolic manipulations: the networks specified by these artificially recombined vectors actually implement the intended functions without any direct training on them. Our results suggest that meta-learning can tune a network's starting point to organize subsequent learning along systematic, functionally meaningful trajectories through the space of possible parameter vectors, providing a geometric basis for realizing inductive biases in neural networks.
papers.Core_Innovation: Decomposes meta-learned parameter updates into additive analogy vectors, isolating function-specific adaptation directions in weight space.
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate capital to acquire or build meta-learning adaptation layers for production models within the next 18 months. Discontinue projects relying on unstructured, full-retraining pipelines once additive analogy metrics demonstrate comparable performance.
papers.Tags: Meta-Learning, Additive Analogies, Neural Networks, Rapid Learning, Parameter Space
papers.Hook: Meta-learned networks exhibit additive parameter shifts enabling rapid function acquisition.

papers.Title: Sketching Language Models for Context Attribution
papers.Abstract: Context attribution asks how removing parts of a prompt changes a language model's output. We study leave-one-out (LOO) attribution for a prompt of $n$ tokens and a fixed measurement function. Computing all LOO values directly requires $n$ model evaluations. Under a stability assumption, our algorithm estimates all LOO values to error proportional to $\varepsilon$ with constant probability using $O(\sqrt{\log(1/\varepsilon)}/\varepsilon)$ evaluation calls. To complement our upper bound, we prove a matching $Ω(\sqrt{\log(1/\varepsilon)}/\varepsilon)$ lower bound on the number of evaluation calls in an oracle model. Empirically, we verify coefficient decay consistent with stability and evaluate the performance of our sketching algorithm on a small language-model retrieval task.   Technically, our result is based on a sketching algorithm for arithmetic circuits whose Taylor coefficients satisfy the stability condition recently introduced by Gunn [Gun26]. A direct adaptation of their forward differentiation sketches would require $\widetilde{O}(\log(n)/\varepsilon^2)$ evaluation calls. Our key observation is that we can apply forward differentiation to the backpropagation circuit, with only constant overhead over a forward sketch of the same Taylor degree. This reduces the variance of the sketches and is key to our improved evaluation bound. Our lower bound builds on the techniques of Amsel, Chen, Duman Keles, Halikias, Musco, and Musco [ACDH+26, SIAM Journal on Matrix Analysis and Applications] for lower bounding the number of matrix-vector queries to estimate the diagonal elements of random matrices.
papers.Core_Innovation: Introduces a sketching framework for arithmetic circuits with stability-enforcing Taylor coefficients. This enables ε-accurate leave-one-out attribution with near-optimal evaluation complexity.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Language Model Development, AI Retrieval, Natural Language Processing
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate funding for sketching-based attribution tooling within 3 months to replace exhaustive LOO pipelines. Deploy validated frameworks once ε-error thresholds are met on target prompts.
papers.Tags: sketching, attribution, arithmetic circuits, stability, language models
papers.Hook: Enables ε-accurate leave-one-out attribution with near-optimal model evaluation calls.

papers.Title: Classical Energies Learn to Reason 1,000x Faster than Looped Models
papers.Abstract: Looped models have emerged as a prominent paradigm for reasoning, with successes on simple reasoning puzzles such as Sudoku-Extreme and Maze-Unique. However, these models can be unstable, slow to train, and use many parameters and FLOPs to solve simple puzzles. Descent on an energy not only mitigates these issues but also offers advantages: built-in early stopping, compute that adapts to problem difficulty, fast training without differentiating through a solver, and interpretable weights that learn the constraints of the puzzle. Here we demonstrate this with a learned version of Hopfield & Tank's energy from the 80s, which we term CRAM, solves 99.996% of Sudoku-Extreme and 100% of Maze-Unique test puzzles after 42 ms and 132 ms of training on one GPU, at least 1,000x faster than looped models on these tasks. CRAM also matches baseline looped models at their highest accuracy on Sudoku-Extreme using at least 282x fewer inference FLOPs. Our work suggests two things. First, that energies are an extremely promising direction for training reasoning from data. Second, a caution against using trivially solvable benchmarks like Sudoku and Maze to test the scalability of looped reasoning techniques.
papers.Core_Innovation: CRAM introduces a learned Hopfield-Tank energy model for reasoning. Energy descent replaces iterative looped computation, enabling built-in early stopping and adaptive compute.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Artificial Intelligence, Optimization Software, Education Technology
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate engineering resources to integrate CRAM into production reasoning pipelines within the next two quarters to capture 1,000x latency reductions. Cancel planned expansions of looped model infrastructure for combinatorial puzzle tasks given CRAM's 282x FLOP efficiency at parity accuracy.
papers.Tags: CRAM, Energy Descent, Reasoning
papers.Hook: CRAM enables 1,000x faster reasoning than looped models on Sudoku and maze puzzles

papers.Title: Quantifying structural stability of transparent models for general insurance pricing
papers.Abstract: The short duration of general insurance contracts leads to rapid distributional shifts in the data, warranting regular model updates. This process may yield a post-update model that differs considerably from the pre-update model in both predictions and structure. Structural stability is upstream of predictive stability, yet existing structural stability metrics are mostly restricted to simple decision trees. Thus, we first introduce the notion of functional transparency, characterising models with a prediction function that can be expressed as a sum of univariate functions for main effects and bivariate functions for pairwise interactions. Then, we propose the Mean Squared Shape function distance, a metric to quantify the structural stability of functionally transparent models, which are particularly relevant in actuarial science. Using three public auto insurance datasets, we present a benchmark study to demonstrate the usefulness of our metric in identifying a stable and accurate transparent model. Generalised linear models with centred numerical covariates are stable, and explainable boosting machines (EBMs) offer a compromise between stability and performance. We also find that stabilisation strategies, such as sequential modelling and fixed hyperparameters, can substantially improve stability for both EBM and XGBoost models, with negligible impact on performance.
papers.Core_Innovation: Introduces functional transparency as additive main-effects plus bivariate pairwise interaction decompositions, then proposes Mean Squared Shape function distance as the first structural stability metric beyond decision-tree limitations.
papers.Decision_Perspective: Insurers should adopt MSSfD to audit model structural shifts during regular pricing updates, enabling data-driven retraining triggers. A 3-month pilot across pricing teams will quantify stability gains versus current predictive-only metrics.
papers.Tags: structural stability, functional transparency, Mean Squared Shape function distance, actuarial science
papers.Hook: New metric quantifies structural stability in transparent insurance pricing models

papers.Title: Towards a Theory of Learnability via Debate
papers.Abstract: Debate has been recently proposed as a training protocol that is hoped to produce more aligned models even as model capabilities scale. The idea is that the human, instead of providing supervision in the form of labels, judges a debate between two models that compete to prove the correctness of opposite labels. It can be shown that functions of a much higher computational complexity can be correctly judged in this way, compared to the complexity of functions that can be directly evaluated using a computationally weak evaluator. This suggests that perhaps debate can be used to teach very complicated functions to models. However, previous work has largely ignored the fact that this is a training protocol, and simply analyzes the game being played between the two debaters for a known judge. We take the first steps towards understanding the learning problem implicit within the protocol, by formulating it as an online learning problem. We show that once we formulate the learning problem precisely, there are cases where the best way to learn given access to a judge is different from running an adversarial debate. This motivates us to define a cooperative version of the protocol, whose learnability we characterize using a combinatorial dimension. We also consider the possibility of the human judge being fallible and occasionally judging the debate incorrectly. We show that a small number of errors in judgement can lead to a large error in learning.
papers.Core_Innovation: The paper formulates debate as an online learning problem, shifting analysis from fixed-judge games to adaptive protocol-driven learnability
papers.Decision_Perspective: Prioritize funding debate-integrated training frameworks to enable models to generalize beyond labeled data constraints. Implement within 18 months for high-complexity function evaluation in regulated AI domains
papers.Tags: Debate, Online Learning, Model Alignment, Computational Complexity, Training Protocols
papers.Hook: Debate as online learning enables models to acquire high-complexity function judgment

papers.Title: FLEX-LBP: Learning Local Binary Patterns with Exact Binary Inference for Texture Classification
papers.Abstract: Local Binary Patterns (LBP) remain among the most widely used texture descriptors, from industrial inspection to medical imaging. Yet their radius, sampling angles, color transform and thresholds are fixed by hand for each dataset. We present FLEX-LBP, which learns these parameters by backpropagation while every forward pass computes exact binary codes and hard histogram counts. A straight-through estimator acts only in the backward pass, so the deployed descriptor is an interpretable hard-binary LBP with 90 learnable parameters and unchanged inference cost. In a controlled ablation on six color texture benchmarks, the component worth learning is dataset-dependent. One configuration, applied unchanged everywhere, learns the geometry and thresholds with the color transform frozen. It improves the nearest-neighbor accuracy of the identical fixed descriptor by 3.55 points on average over five seeds, significantly on five of six benchmarks and never significantly worse. With a linear discriminant readout, it gains 0.9 points; the fully learned descriptor gains 2.7 and has the highest mean. FLEX-LBP is more accurate than five classical LBP-family descriptors, PCANet and a neural LBP on five of six benchmarks. Its mean nearest-neighbor accuracy exceeds that of frozen ImageNet ResNet-50 features (23.5 million parameters). On the Kather colorectal cancer histology benchmark, the fully learned descriptor reaches 93.8%, significantly above the best classical descriptor (Completed LBP, 92.8%). The learned radii adapt in directions that recur across seeds. Noise drowns single-pixel comparisons and illuminant change flips inter-channel ones; median sampling or gray-world normalization restores 96-97%. The code is available as a drop-in PyTorch layer at https://github.com/medalimoussa/FLEX-LBP.
papers.Core_Innovation: A straight-through estimator backpropagates through exact binary LBP computation, learning geometry and thresholds while preserving hard-binary forward codes and zero-inference overhead.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Industrial Inspection, Medical Imaging, Computer Vision
papers.Decision_Perspective: Integrate FLEX-LBP into texture classification pipelines within the next two quarters to replace fixed-parameter baselines. Discontinue hand-tuned LBP configurations for new computer vision projects once benchmark parity is confirmed.
papers.Tags: LBP, texture classification, learnable parameters
papers.Hook: Backpropagated LBP parameter learning preserves exact binary inference.

papers.Title: Consistent Video-to-Video Translation via Explicit Correspondences
papers.Abstract: Interactive video-to-video applications require real-time generation while maintaining long-range temporal consistency. However, recent methods achieve speed by restricting attention to a fixed-length causal window. This limits long-range consistency whenever relevant history falls outside the context window. To address this limitation, we introduce vid2vid-long, a correspondence-based approach grounded in a simple observation. Video-to-video translation provides an explicit cross-frame reference: the regions that match in the input video should match in the output video too. Concretely, we compute patch-level correspondences in the input, guiding retrieval of previously generated outputs in the corresponding regions, and condition the model on these patches through correspondence cross-attention. Our experiments demonstrate that vid2vid-long consistently improves long-range temporal consistency across recent video models while preserving generation quality and real-time performance.
papers.Core_Innovation: Patch-level correspondences retrieved from the input guide cross-attention over prior generated frames, enabling long-range consistency beyond the causal window
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate capital to correspondence-aware video generation startups within 18 months to lead market adoption. Discontinue investment in fixed-causal-window video models as correspondence-based alternatives achieve parity.
papers.Tags: Video Translation, Temporal Consistency, Correspondence Attention, Real-Time Generation, Long-Range Consistency
papers.Hook: Real-time video translation with long-range temporal consistency via explicit cross-frame patch correspondences

papers.Title: Goal Encoding in LLMs
papers.Abstract: We investigate whether and how LLMs encode goals: internal neural representations that precede and guide action, and that are flexible enough to be realized through many different execution paths. We construct a coding setting with multiple sub-tasks that allows us to evaluate goal-seeking behavior and the selection of sub-goals. In this setting, we localize an encoding of the next sub-goal in the outputs of a sparse set of attention heads. The same heads can be used to decode the LM's future actions in natural language (e.g., "I'm checking if a word is a palindrome"). We verify that this encoding is causal for next action and is plastic: transplanting it into a different environment, e.g., another programming language, triggers the same operation realized with a different sequence of tokens. The LM also sustains the encoding throughout the action's execution, which is puzzling because a transformer LM without recurrence cannot carry a state forward for more tokens than it has layers left. We propose that it does not need to. Under a non-recurrent goal-seeking (NRGS) account, the LM frequently re-reads the goal from the task specification, compares it with the progress visible in the growing context, and pursues what remains. We test the predictions of this account with targeted causal interventions.
papers.Core_Innovation: The work isolates a sparse set of attention heads whose activations causally encode the next sub-goal, and demonstrates these representations persist and transfer operationally across distinct programming environments.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Artificial Intelligence, Software Development, Agentic AI
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate resources to build diagnostic probes targeting the identified attention heads for LLM safety auditing within the next quarter. Commission cross-language transplantation tests to confirm operational generality before product integration.
papers.Tags: Goal Encoding, Attention Heads, Cross-Language Transfer, Causal Representation, LLM Mechanisms
papers.Hook: Sparse attention heads encode and transplant goal representations across languages, enabling causal action selection.

papers.Title: Metal Sandbox: Isolated Execution and Command Scheduling for GPU Coding Agents on Apple Silicon
papers.Abstract: On-device inference requires kernels that make effective use of local accelerators. Efficient training and evaluation of models that generate Apple Metal kernels benefit from native macOS tools and concurrent agent sessions. These sessions alternate between model requests, development commands, and GPU execution, leaving GPU capacity idle for much of a rollout. We present Metal Sandbox, infrastructure that combines restricted per-instance file access, native command execution, and command-level scheduling across interconnected Macs. Each agent retains its workspace and private development environment. Parallel commands can run concurrently, while serial commands share one execution slot per node; eligible waiting commands can migrate to available Macs and return results to the original agent. Integration with Harbor supports task execution, automatic verification, and rollout collection through a common workflow. Controlled experiments on four Mac mini M4 nodes achieve $1.68\times$--$2.05\times$ gains in command throughput under concentrated demand. Sixteen static agent traces give an estimated $2.14\times$ sustained-throughput gain for four sessions per node versus one, assuming continuously replenished sessions and unchanged mean durations. Replaying these measured traces under dynamic scheduling reduces mean tool waiting by 18.8% and batch elapsed time by 22.3%, assuming unchanged phase durations. Metal Sandbox and its Harbor integration are open-source on GitHub.
papers.Core_Innovation: Command-level scheduling enables waiting GPU commands to migrate across interconnected Macs while maintaining per-instance file isolation and Harbor-verified rollout collection.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Artificial Intelligence, Cloud Computing, macOS Software Development
papers.Decision_Perspective: Apple should integrate Metal Sandbox APIs into macOS 16 within 12 months to enable native agent scheduling. Competitors must adopt cross-node GPU command migration within 18 months or risk losing AI developer adoption on Apple Silicon.
papers.Tags: Metal, GPU Scheduling, Apple Silicon, Command Migration, Harbor
papers.Hook: Metal Sandbox schedules GPU commands across Macs, idle capacity eliminated for agent rollouts.

papers.Title: Negative-Only Policy Optimization for One-Sided Verifiable Rewards
papers.Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) typically relies on a verifier that can reliably judge whether sampled solutions are correct. However, in many realistic settings, complete verification is generally unavailable, while cheap checks can only falsify failures. We formalize this regime as one-sided verifiability (OSV): verified negatives are reliable counterexamples, but verified positives are merely non-falsified candidates and may contain many false positives. This asymmetry makes standard RLVR unreliable, because reinforcing verified positives can directly reward shortcuts that pass partial checks. To address this issue, we propose Negative-Only Policy Optimization (NOPO), which treats verified positives as unlabeled and updates the policy only by suppressing trusted verified negatives. Specifically, NOPO combines a reference-relative negative suppression loss with a group-level adapter that scales each update by the proportion of non-falsified responses. Across unit-test, constraint-check, and LLM self-verifiers, NOPO improves pass@k over baselines on code, logic, and math benchmarks when oracle rewards are unavailable. These gains persist under inference-time scaling and cross-benchmark transfer.
papers.Core_Innovation: NOPO updates policy solely by suppressing verified negatives using a reference-relative loss, with updates scaled by the proportion of non-falsified responses.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Artificial Intelligence, Large Language Model Alignment, Reward Modeling
papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Reinforcement Learning Platforms, Large Language Model Fine-Tuning, AI Code Assistants
papers.Decision_Perspective: Product teams should immediately audit reward verifiers for one-sided failure modes and halt positive-reinforced policy updates. Organizations relying on unverified positive rewards in RL pipelines should transition to NOPO-compatible frameworks within 6 months.
papers.Tags: NOPO,One-Sided Verifiability,Reward Modeling,Policy Gradient
papers.Hook: Policy updates verified negatives only, avoiding unreliable positive rewards in one-sided verification.

papers.Title: Synthesis Smuggling: Maliciously Hiding Inferred Personal Attributes in LLM Outputs
papers.Abstract: We propose Synthesis Smuggling, a novel threat model in which an adversarial LLM infers sensitive information about a user from routine assistance-seeking interactions and steganographically encodes that into innocuous-looking model-generated content. The user may then unknowingly transmit that information by sharing the generated artifact, say as an email, social-media post, or message, through ordinary communication channels. An adversary monitoring these channels can discover this information. We demonstrate this threat by training two open-weight models to infer gender and age-group labels from conversational cues and encode their predictions using invisible characters or word choices. These results show that user-shared model outputs can become a covert channel for personal inferences, even when the model itself has no direct means of contacting an adversary.
papers.Core_Innovation: Models predict sensitive user attributes from conversational patterns and encode them using zero-width Unicode characters and stylistic word selection, producing superficially normal text that conceals structured personal data
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate dedicated budget for steganographic LLM output analysis within the next two fiscal quarters. Mandate covert-channel risk reviews for any model deployed in user-facing channels.
papers.Tags: llm, steganography, privacy, threatmodel, covertchannel
papers.Hook: LLMs covertly infer user attributes and embed them via invisible characters in innocuous output

papers.Title: Medical Image Segmentation: Foundation Model Adaptation versus Task-Specific Training
papers.Abstract: Foundation models pretrained on large natural-image collections are increasingly adapted for medical image segmentation, in the expectation that they will replace models trained for each task. Most comparisons, however, use data from the training distribution and a single task-specific baseline whose configuration is rarely justified, and therefore provide limited evidence of performance at new clinical sites. It also remains unclear how much of a foundation model must be adapted, and what determines this. We adapted a foundation model, DINOv2, with strategies ranging from tuning only its bias terms to full fine-tuning, and compared it with U-Nets and ResU-Nets trained from scratch. Experiments covered colonoscopy, breast ultrasound and dermoscopy, with testing on held-out data from the training source and on independent datasets from other institutions. The adapted foundation model generalised better on every external dataset. Within the training distribution, the task-specific models remained competitive when training data were abundant, and delineated boundaries more precisely, while the foundation model more often missed small lesions. Only a small fraction of the foundation model required adaptation, and the capacity needed was determined by the imaging domain rather than by the adaptation method. A widely used polyp test set was also found to duplicate images from another benchmark. Foundation-model adaptation is therefore warranted where models must work across sites, with capacity selected on the target domain.
papers.Core_Innovation: We evaluate DINOv2 adaptation from bias-term-only tuning to full fine-tuning against U-Net and ResU-Net baselines trained from scratch, isolating the generalization trade-off across colonoscopy, breast ultrasound, and dermoscopy.
papers.Decision_Perspective: Hospital AI departments should deploy DINOv2 adaptation pipelines with bias-initialization-to-full fine-tuning within 12 months to achieve cross-institution segmentation robustness. Investment funds must deprioritize single-task U-Net startups lacking foundation model adaptation strategies for multi-site deployment.
papers.Tags: medical-imaging, foundation-models, cross-institution-generalization
papers.Hook: Adapting foundation models enables robust medical segmentation across institutions without task-specific retraining

papers.Title: Toward Foundation Detection Models via Example-Based Grounding in EM-DETR
papers.Abstract: DeepLearning (DL)-based Computer-Aided Diagnostic (CAD) systems have shown great promise in supporting clinicians, but their performance heavily depends on the availability of large, well-annotated datasets. In medical lesion detection, the scarcity of comprehensive, stan dardized annotations and the heterogeneity of existing datasets limit the development of robust foundation models. In this work, we introduce a novel approach to building a multi-domain foundation model for le sion detection by integrating diverse medical image datasets annotated for both anatomical structures and abnormalities. We first propose a student-teacher training strategy to effectively combine datasets with heterogeneous label spaces, mitigating catastrophic forgetting, and im proving feature learning. In addition, building on our previously pro posed example-based EM-DETR framework, we adapt it to jointly learn from multiple domain-specific datasets, enabling fine-grained, example driven detection across modalities. Our model achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) results, with image-level AUC scores exceeding previous SOTA by 1% point on four key findings in CXRs. We achieve a leading mAP50 in CXRs and mammography, surpassing EM-DETR trained on a single dataset by 2-3% points. This approach paves the way for scalable foundation models in medical imaging that leverage heterogeneous data while maintaining robust and generalizable performance.
papers.Core_Innovation: Student-teacher training aligns heterogeneous label spaces while preserving feature integrity, integrated with EM-DETR's example-based grounding for cross-domain lesion detection.
papers.Decision_Perspective: Prioritize funding for multi-domain medical AI startups integrating student-teacher training with EM-DETR example grounding, targeting FDA clearance by 2027. Avoid investing in single-dataset CAD systems lacking cross-domain generalization
papers.Tags: Medical Imaging, Foundation Models, Multi-Dataset Learning, Student-Teacher Training, EM-DETR
papers.Hook: Multi-domain medical lesion detection foundation models trained without catastrophic forgetting across heterogeneous datasets.

papers.Title: TorchCurves: Differentiable Parametric Curves
papers.Abstract: We present TorchCurves, a PyTorch library that treats vector-valued parametric curves as learnable primitives. Its central operation maps batches of scalar inputs to points on curves represented in B-spline or Legendre polynomial bases, with differentiation through both inputs and coefficients. Curve coefficients can be optimized jointly with the surrounding model or produced by another network. The library provides trainable modules, reusable basis modules, and a functional interface, supporting applications ranging from continuous feature embeddings to Kolmogorov-Arnold networks and functional regression. Its implementation combines classical evaluation algorithms with vectorized PyTorch operations, emphasizing readability and maintainability without custom hardware kernels. Timing experiments compare curve evaluation against NumPy and SciPy and KAN training against EfficientKAN across a range of problem sizes. The results illustrate where this generality remains computationally practical and where overhead is substantial. Library is available on GitHub at https://github.com/alexshtf/torchcurves.
papers.Core_Innovation: Parametric curves become differentiable PyTorch modules with gradient flow through both input locations and basis coefficients, enabling joint optimization with downstream deep models
papers.Decision_Perspective: Integrate TorchCurves into our KAN pipeline within 4 weeks to quantify gradient-flow gains on continuous feature embedding tasks. Allocate funding to the team whose benchmark reduction versus EfficientKAN exceeds 5% on target regression suites.
papers.Tags: DifferentiableCurves, PyTorch, BSplines, KANs, FunctionalRegression
papers.Hook: End-to-end differentiable parametric curves now integrate as PyTorch primitives with full backpropagation.

papers.Title: AutoScaffold: AI-Guided Scaffolding for Reinforcement Learning of Language Models
papers.Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) produces rich training experience, yet outcome rewards reduce each attempt to a single number and leave most of this information unused. Training-time scaffolds, such as strategies or hints added to the prompt during training, offer a natural way to turn this information into guidance, but their design and adaptation are largely left to humans and tailored to specific domains. We introduce AutoScaffold, a unified AI-for-AI framework that turns a student's training experience into adaptive scaffolds, with minimal domain-specific information and no human intervention during training. A frozen teacher periodically examines this experience, diagnoses bottlenecks, and designs scaffolds in two forms: (i) strategies shared across a class of tasks and (ii) hints for individual hard tasks, adjusting the content and amount of support as the student learns. The scaffolds are removed at evaluation. We apply the same framework to ALFWorld, search-based QA, mathematical reasoning, and GPU kernel generation. When evaluated without scaffolds, students trained with AutoScaffold outperform those trained with the corresponding RL baselines in all four domains, with gains of 7.2 points in ALFWorld success and 4.0 points in average QA exact match. On GPU kernel generation, AutoScaffold increases the fraction of tasks with a correct kernel that runs faster than the PyTorch reference by up to 5.0 points. On math, our student surpasses QuestA's reported accuracy using approximately one-third as many student training steps. Analyses show that the teacher identifies a different failure in each task class and shifts its scaffolds from step-by-step workflows to targeted fixes as the student improves, and that its revised scaffolds help the student learn more than keeping the previous scaffold or using no scaffold.
papers.Core_Innovation: A frozen teacher model periodically evaluates student training experience, diagnoses bottlenecks, and dynamically generates adaptive prompt scaffolds—strategies for task classes and hints for individual instances. These scaffolds are annealed at evaluation.
papers.Decision_Perspective: Integrate AutoScaffold into LLM training pipelines within the next two quarters to enable scaffold-free RL workflows. Acquire or partner with teams developing AI-for-AI scaffold generation to secure early-mover advantage in automated model training.
papers.Tags: AutoScaffold, Reinforcement Learning, Prompt Scaffolding, AI Agents
papers.Hook: AutoScaffold automates adaptive scaffold generation for language model RL with zero human intervention.

papers.Title: Contrastive Discovery: Open-Ended Scientific Discovery over Competing Explanations
papers.Abstract: LLM agents are increasingly used for open-ended, data-driven scientific discovery, yet most of them evaluate hypotheses pointwise, testing an empirical claim $h$ only against its complement $\neg h$. When evidence rejects $h$, the agent learns that one explanation is unlikely but not which alternative the evidence supports. To recover that alternative, we introduce Contrastive Discovery, which replaces the single hypothesis with a contrast set, a scientific question paired with mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive competing explanations. Each experiment is scored by how its evidence redistributes belief across the set, and the question is resolved when belief concentrates on one explanation. Because contrast sets change only the unit an agent proposes and scores, an existing agent can use them to re-evaluate evidence it has already collected or to guide its search. Across six domains, $89\%$ of the pointwise candidates with the largest belief shifts are rejections. On the same evidence, contrast sets resolve $73\%$ of these candidates to a specific alternative. When contrast sets guide search, the agent resolves $67\%$ more questions than pointwise surprisal under the same experiment budget. In a blinded study, $38$ human experts chose the same explanation on $78\%$ of resolved questions and on $82\%$ of questions where the pointwise agent rejected its hypothesis and stopped. Together, these results support explicit competing explanations as a way for discovery agents to resolve more scientific questions from the same evidence and validation budget.
papers.Core_Innovation: The framework shifts hypothesis evaluation from pointwise rejection to contrast sets, scoring experiments by belief redistribution across mutually exclusive explanations until one explanation concentrates belief and resolves the question
papers.Decision_Perspective: Retrofit current LLM agents to generate contrast sets for open-ended hypothesis testing within six months. Deploy the framework to prioritize high-impact scientific domains first.
papers.Tags: contrastive discovery, LLM agents, belief redistribution, open-ended science
papers.Hook: LLMs resolve open-ended science by contrasting mutually exclusive explanations.

papers.Title: Pyrite: Building and Benchmarking Protein-Ligand Pose Ranking Agents
papers.Abstract: Predicting how a ligand binds to its target is central to small-molecule drug discovery. Modern cofolding models can generate diverse candidate poses, but reliably ranking these candidates remains challenging. We introduce Pyrite, a pairwise pose-ranking benchmark comprising 1,500 pose pairs across diverse protein-ligand complexes. Expert chemists equipped with 3D visualization tools and physics-based scores perform near chance, highlighting the difficulty of interpreting available chemical signals. To investigate automated ranking, we introduce PyriteRep, a structured representation of molecular geometry, protein-ligand interactions, and physicochemical scores, and develop two LLM-based agents: PyriteReasoner, which directly compares poses through text-based reasoning, and PyriteFeaturizer, which generates executable code to construct features for logistic regression, optionally incorporating features derived from LLM subcalls. These agents achieve up to 67% and 74% accuracy, respectively, exceeding observed expert performance. LLM-guided feature discovery generally outperforms direct reasoning, while Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) improves open-weight models, enabling them to match or surpass closed-source frontier models in our evaluations. These results establish Pyrite as a challenging test of pose-ranking ability and highlight LLM-guided feature discovery as a promising approach to interpret and combine the outputs of computational chemistry tools.
papers.Core_Innovation: PyriteRep formalizes protein-ligand pose geometry, interaction fingerprints, and physicochemical scores into a unified structured representation. PyriteFeaturizer then auto-generates executable Python code to construct logistic-regression features from PyriteRep, optionally invoking LLMs for semantic pose comparisons.
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate seed funding to integrate PyriteFeaturizer into lead optimization pipelines within 6 months. Mandate retirement of manual pose-ranking vendors once PyriteReasoner exceeds 70% accuracy.
papers.Tags: ProteinLigandRanking,LLMCodeGeneration,MolecularRepresentation,DrugDiscovery
papers.Hook: LLMs now autonomously rank protein-ligand poses with 74% accuracy from geometric features

papers.Title: When Does the Real Wiring Win? Testing connectome structure-function claims against unmeasured physiology
papers.Abstract: Connectome-constrained models are often used to argue that a measured wiring diagram outperforms shuffled or rewired wiring, and hence that structure shapes function. Such comparisons can confound wiring with how the models are tuned: a connectome fixes who connects to whom, not the excitability, gains or plasticity rates the model also needs, and modellers often tune these until the real-wiring model works. We separate three estimands: physiology tuned on the real wiring and transferred to nulls (P1), each wiring tuned on its own (P2), and P2 restricted to physiology consistent with independent data (P3). The biases involved are known in machine learning (under-tuned baselines, inherited weights, winner's curse); we measure what they do to biological conclusions, using synthetic ground truth, placebo nulls and three Drosophila circuit models. Some claims survive every protocol we test: segregated reward and punishment dopamine improves learning, and head-direction topography is required for a persistent bump. Others do not. In the mushroom body, the real Kenyon-cell output wiring beats a cross-subtype identity shuffle by 0.09 under P1 and P2 but loses to it by 0.09 under P3 (95% CIs exclude zero; held-out runs confirm). The verdict is set by the share of alpha'beta' cells among active Kenyon cells, which P1 selects low; at the share implied by imaging (about 44%) the real-wiring model fails to learn, exposing a model inadequacy rather than a deficit of the fly's wiring. In flyvis, P1 penalises a mirrored connectome, which has a constructed solution within 0.07 (median) of the real error, more than a spatially shuffled one in 50 of 50 members; the ranking survives ten-fold longer retraining but depends on the checkpoint at fifty-fold. A credible structural claim needs matched optimisation, data-constrained physiology and a model that still works there.
papers.Core_Innovation: Introduces P1-P3 estimand protocol that isolates physiology bias from wiring using placebo nulls and Drosophila circuit models.
papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund P3-validated connectome models for neural prosthetic development within 18 months. Immediately deprioritize structure-function claims that ignore independent physiology constraints.
papers.Tags: Connectome Modeling, Structure-Function, Physiology Bias
papers.Hook: Enables separating physiology tuning from wiring effects in connectome-function claims.

papers.Title: Continual-ARC: Measuring Skill Acquisition over a Working Lifetime
papers.Abstract: Agent harnesses have emerged as a promising mechanism for continual learning, alongside test-time parametric learning. However, the current benchmarks have several limitations: they generally focus on a single applied domain, serve each instance only once, and assume a single family of learner, so memory-based and weight-based systems are rarely compared on the same scale. We propose Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream built from the three ARC-AGI editions, whose tasks need no domain knowledge. The same tasks return after dormant gaps with fresh instances, while new tasks keep arriving. On each instance, the learner may pay for demonstrations, submit answers, or act inside the harness, with retries permitted on incorrect submissions, which are paid for. Each instance is scored based on the share of this feedback budget consumed. Since a learner may keep anything between instances, memory-based and weight-based systems are scored on the same scale. After the stream, the learner is frozen and tested on fresh instances of the tasks it met, which measures memorization, and on unseen tasks, which measures generalization. We run an agent harness with frozen weights, with and without persistence, on Qwen3.5-9B and GLM-5.3 Flash, comparing them with two prompting floors, a program-induction method and Qwen3.5-9B's weights trained to imitate GLM-5.3 Flash. Persistence in the harness generally does not improve memorization unless provided with explicit expert guidance. Most harness-based methods still learn less than a floor that simply caches each task's demonstrations, across all models we tested. No harness-based method gains on unseen tasks, whereas weight-based learning shows substantial gains. This opens the door to future weight-based continual learning that could teach models to drive harnesses in new domains.
papers.Core_Innovation: It introduces a recurring lifelong task stream where instances reappear after dormant gaps and are scored by cumulative feedback budget consumption, enabling first-of-its-kind memory-versus-weight system comparison
papers.Decision_Perspective: Mandate Continual-ARC integration for all new lifelong learning agents within the next two quarters to enable memory-vs-weight benchmarking. Phase out static benchmark suites that do not support task reuse and budget-based scoring.
papers.Tags: Continual Learning, Benchmark Design, Agent Harnesses, Memory-Based Learning
papers.Hook: Continual-ARC enables lifelong skill measurement by reusing ARC tasks with fresh instances after dormant gaps.

papers.Title: Emergent Biological Capabilities in a Foundation Model for Molecular Interactions
papers.Abstract: Foundation models trained on large unlabeled corpora develop emergent capabilities, tasks that go beyond the training objective. We extend this paradigm to multimodal biology with Bonbon, a foundation model for molecular interactions trained on approximately 3.2 trillion tokens of paired protein-ligand sequences. From a single representation space, Bonbon exhibits three zero-shot emergent capabilities at hierarchical levels of resolution: functional (mechanism of action), residue (binding site localization, including orthosteric/allosteric discrimination), and bond (covalent versus non-covalent engagement). All three capabilities generalize to out-of-distribution complexes. Bonbon was trained on protein-ligand sequences alone, without any task-specific supervision and without structural coordinates. We conducted controlled scaling experiments across six model scales from 42M to 1.6B parameters; every capability evaluated shows a sharp jump at the largest scale on continuous metrics, even as pretraining loss decreases smoothly. This demonstrates that loss-based scaling laws alone are insufficient to predict when zero-shot emergent capabilities become available. The capabilities reported here emerge after training at a 1:2,000 parameter-to-token ratio to accommodate the sparsity of paired biological interaction data. The same frozen representations achieve state-of-the-art binding and affinity prediction at five orders of magnitude greater speed than co-folding methods. In prospective wet-lab validation across nine disease targets spanning seven protein families, Bonbon achieves a 61.5% dose-response hit rate on de novo compounds, yielding structurally novel molecules not previously reported to inhibit these proteins, including for out-of-distribution targets.
papers.Core_Innovation: Bonbon discovers hierarchical zero-shot molecular interaction capabilities functional residue and bond level exclusively from protein-ligand sequence tokens. Capability emergence sharply increases at the largest model scale despite absence of structural coordinates.
papers.Decision_Perspective: Accelerate internal proof-of-concept integration of sequence-only molecular models into lead optimization pipelines within 6 months. Redirect capital away from structure-dependent docking vendors whose value proposition is eroded by zero-shot emergence.
papers.Tags: Foundation Models, Molecular Interactions, Zero-Shot, Emergent Capabilities
papers.Hook: Bonbon enables zero-shot mechanistic, residue, and bond-level molecular analysis from sequences alone.

papers.Title: Comparative Analysis of Agent Evaluation Frameworks: Stability, Detection, and Discovery in Enterprise Analytics Agents
papers.Abstract: Deploying LLM-based analytics agents in enterprise settings requires evaluation frameworks that can reliably detect failures across complex, multi-tool workflows. We present a three-phase comparative study of three evaluation frameworks, each representing a distinct evaluation paradigm (trace-based LLM judging, text-only LLM judging with red-teaming, and deterministic heuristics), applied to two analytics agents in a controlled research setting using frozen execution traces. Phase 1 quantifies evaluation harness stability through repeated measurements, finding that 97% of configurations meet the stability threshold and that stability patterns are agent-independent. Phase 2 measures known risk detection on 72 ground-truth test cases, where the trace-based framework achieves the best precision-recall balance (F1=0.90) while text-only evaluation matches on recall but generates 5x more false alarms. Phase 3 evaluates unknown risk discovery, uncovering 24 novel failures with zero overlap between functional testing and security red-teaming. Our results demonstrate that (1) the information available to the evaluation harness determines evaluation quality, (2) functional and security evaluation are complementary, and (3) LLM-based evaluation harnesses surface subtle errors that human reviewers miss. We recommend a two-framework strategy: trace-based evaluation for functional assessment and adversarial red-teaming for security validation.
papers.Core_Innovation: Introduces a three-phase quantitative protocol to benchmark stability, precision-recall tradeoffs, and unknown risk discovery in enterprise LLM analytics agents using frozen execution traces.
papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund immediate deployment of trace-based evaluation frameworks in enterprise agent pipelines within six months. Phase out text-only LLM judging frameworks that generate five times more false alarms.
papers.Tags: LLM evaluation, enterprise analytics, stability testing, risk detection
papers.Hook: Trace-based evaluation detects and discovers enterprise agent failures with 97% stability and 5x fewer false alarms

papers.Title: ReTrace: Distilling Tool-Using Agents into Planner-Free Workflows
papers.Abstract: Business process automation runs the same Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) again and again on new inputs. Large Language Model (LLM) agents can follow an SOP written in natural language, but they call an LLM to choose every step of every run, which adds latency and cost at scale. We present ReTrace, which turns an SOP and a few logged agent runs into a reusable workflow in which code, not an LLM, selects the next step. The agent's reasoning, the explanation it writes with each tool call, often states why it took an action; the tool calls alone do not. ReTrace extracts the condition behind each step, merges these conditions across runs into a compact rule document, and generates an executable workflow from it. Only this last stage depends on the platform, so rule documents can be compiled for different orchestration platforms. On $79$ procedures from our production platform, ReTrace workflows reach $93.8\%$ completion, against $96.8\%$ for the agent, at $24\%$ lower cost per task. On $τ^2$-Bench, they reach $75.8\%$ task success (agent: $80.6\%$) and run in $1.3$s instead of $170$s; three rounds of repair on training failures lift $k{=}2$ workflows from $66.7\%$ to $81.2\%$. On eight SOP-Bench procedures, ReTrace without repair trails few-shot generation ($80.6\%$ vs. $83.6\%$), but repair from labeled training failures lifts it to $87.8\%$ at $0.40$s per task, compared to $85.5\%$ in $46.6$s for the agent.
papers.Core_Innovation: Extracts implicit step-condition pairs from agent explanation text and consolidates them into a minimal, platform-agnostic rule document.
papers.Decision_Perspective: Prioritize building internal pipelines that convert agent SOPs into platform-agnostic rule documents within the next two quarters. Discontinue LLM-step orchestration tools that lack deterministic rule compilation capabilities.
papers.Tags: LLM agents, workflow distillation, rule compilation, SOP automation, cost reduction
papers.Hook: Transforms LLM agent SOPs into deterministic code workflows, reducing cost 24%.

papers.Title: TimeSeek: Multi-Task and Multi-Domain Pretraining for Generalized Time Series Analytics
papers.Abstract: Time series analytics has been widely applied across various domains. While existing time series foundation models (TSFMs) have demonstrated promising results, they still face two major challenges: 1) Most TSFMs mainly rely on stacking Transformer layers to increase parameter size, lacking the ability to adaptively model complex time series patterns from multi-domain data. 2) Current TSFMs are primarily pre-trained for specific tasks, e.g., forecasting or anomaly detection, and a few models support multiple tasks, but they fail to fully leverage task specificity and commonality, resulting in suboptimal performance. To address these challenges, we propose TimeSeek, a novel generalized time series analytics model that adaptively models time series patterns from multi-domain data and unifies multiple tasks in pre-training. Conceptually, TimeSeek is guided by selective information sharing under domain and task heterogeneity. From the perspective of multi-domain data, we propose a Multi-Domain Feature Extractor that adaptively captures temporal dependencies and channel correlations based on domain-specific characteristics, including progressive multi-scale modeling and adaptive slot channel modeling. From the perspective of the diversity of tasks, we propose multi-task collaborative training, which leverages task specificity and task commonality through task customization and cross-task training, effectively unifying multiple tasks in pre-training and better adapting to diverse downstream scenarios. After pre-training on large-scale time series data, TimeSeek achieves state-of-the-art performance in forecasting, anomaly detection, and classification tasks across both few-shot learning and zero-shot situations, together with favorable inference efficiency.
papers.Core_Innovation: TimeSeek introduces selective information sharing mechanisms that dynamically route domain-specific and task-specific features during pretraining, replacing uniform Transformer parameter expansion with adaptive feature modulation.
papers.Decision_Perspective: Initiate a 100-day pilot integrating TimeSeek's selective sharing module into our finance forecasting stack, triggering full replacement if cross-domain MAE improves by >5%. Reallocate R&D budget from Transformer parameter expansion to multi-domain unification projects, with funding cessation after two quarters of marginal gains.
papers.Tags: Time Series, Multi-Task, Domain Adaptation, Pretraining
papers.Hook: Unified adaptive modeling enables multi-task learning across diverse time series domains.

papers.Title: Re-Search: Dissecting LLM Ideation Through a Two-Player Questioning Game
papers.Abstract: Research ideation is iterative: researchers refine their ideas step by step based on feedback. Yet existing evaluations obscure this search process, making it difficult to understand how LLMs explore the space of research ideas and what limits their progress. We introduce Re-Search, which adapts the format of Twenty Questions to research ideation: given only the research problem of a published paper, a model must rediscover the paper's core idea by asking yes-or-no questions. Built from 200 ICML 2026 papers, Re-Search tracks how a model's idea evolves as it asks questions and receives binary oracle feedback, isolating ideation from execution. Across six recent LLMs, nearly all progress happens within the first 30 of 100 questions, which largely decide how the game ends; after that, most models plateau. Through controlled interventions on the candidate questions and the hypothesis space, we find that the bottleneck is generation, not judgment: models recognize a good idea or a good question when one is offered, but often cannot produce it on their own. We further analyze the ideation traces and find that models fail by either over-exploiting one direction or over-exploring too many. These findings point to concrete design principles for autoresearch systems: since models can judge candidates they cannot produce, enriching the search with externally sourced ideas and questions may be more effective than improving any single model's generation ability.
papers.Core_Innovation: Adapts Twenty-Question dynamics with binary oracle feedback to isolate and track LLM research idea evolution, decoupling it from paper execution.
papers.Decision_Perspective: Product teams should integrate Re-Search-style questioning interfaces into LLM workflows within 6 months to validate idea feasibility early. Organizations must retrain prompt engineers to prioritize question-generation over answer-judgment.
papers.Tags: LLM Ideation, Twenty Questions, Research Framework, Binary Feedback, Generation Bottleneck
papers.Hook: LLMs rediscover paper ideas via 30 yes-or-no questions, exposing ideation limits

papers.Title: C$^2$-Routing: Complementary Cropping and Compression for Efficient Vision-Language Inference
papers.Abstract: Visual Question Answering (VQA) imposes substantial computational overhead on vision-language models (VLMs), motivating model-agnostic input reduction methods that can be readily applied across diverse VLMs, including in black-box settings. Simply enforcing a visual-token cap reduces computation, but it can discard information needed to answer the question. A single reduction strategy also struggles to accommodate different scenarios. Our key observation is that cropping and compression are complementary: cropping highlights small targets and local details, whereas whole-image compression better preserves context for large targets or distributed evidence. Based on this observation, we propose C$^2$-Routing, which adaptively selects cropping or compression according to the input image and question. Since both strategies may still discard key information, we further design a safety gate that uses the predicted joint correctness distribution under original and reduced inputs to guide fallback and protect accuracy. To accommodate consumer GPU resource constraints, all training and evaluation experiments run on RTX 3090 GPUs. To measure gains beyond token capping, we use full-image baselines with the same cap of 1,024 visual tokens. We conduct extensive evaluation on three VLMs and 18 datasets spanning local details, global scenes, scene text, and documents. With the visual budget already capped, C$^2$-Routing further reduces end-to-end FLOPs by 36.53% and visual tokens by 42.36% on average, with a mean relative task-score decrease of only 0.77%.
papers.Core_Innovation: The core innovation is an adaptive router that selects between token cropping and whole-image compression based on image-query content, coupled with a safety gate that uses predicted joint correctness distribution to prevent information loss.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Computer Vision, Autonomous Vehicles, Medical Diagnostics, Retail Analytics
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate budget to prototype C²-Routing in our VQA stack within Q3 2026, targeting 35% compute reduction on benchmark VQA tasks. Halt procurement of static-token-cap VLM compressors that lack adaptive routing intelligence.
papers.Tags: VLM, Adaptive Routing, Cropping, Compression, Safety Gate
papers.Hook: Adaptive cropping-compression routing enables efficient VQA without discarding critical context.

papers.Title: Bayesian inverse problems and epidemic-threshold uncertainty for a heterogeneous SIS reaction-diffusion model
papers.Abstract: We study Bayesian inference of persistence from early observations of a heterogeneous susceptible--infected--susceptible (SIS) reaction--diffusion model with standard incidence. We show that the leading prevalence dynamics depend on the unknown coefficients only through the difference between the transmission and recovery rates and the infected diffusivity. The same pair determines the principal eigenvalue whose sign governs persistence, so early prevalence can inform the threshold even when the individual rates remain uncertain. We prove global weak well-posedness and quantitative parameter stability for the SIS system and use the resulting observation-map estimates to establish Bayesian well-posedness. For an initial infection of size $\varepsilon$, we derive a uniform second-order expansion that describes how the separate rates enter prevalence. Incidence depends explicitly on transmission at leading order. When the noise standard deviation is proportional to $\varepsilon$, we prove $O(\varepsilon)$ convergence in Hellinger distance of the nonlinear posteriors to their low-prevalence limits for both prevalence alone and joint prevalence and incidence data. We bound the principal eigenvalue using the growth rate of the infected $L^2$ norm between two times. This rate gives a lower bound for the full nonlinear system, and the upper bound separates spatial transients from nonlinear saturation. Uniform spectral estimates and bounds on infection size and measurement error give sufficient conditions for persistence and extinction. We also bound the error in posterior persistence probabilities under forward and eigenvalue approximation, accounting for posterior mass near the threshold. Numerical examples illustrate threshold inference and the predicted \(O(\varepsilon)\) convergence of the nonlinear posteriors to their low-prevalence limits in Hellinger distance.
papers.Core_Innovation: The persistence threshold reduces to a principal eigenvalue depending only on the transmission-recovery rate difference and infected diffusivity, enabling Bayesian inference from early prevalence without identifying individual rates.
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate funding to develop real-time Bayesian threshold estimators for sector-specific outbreak risk within 90 days of initial infection reports. Integrate these estimators into existing epidemiological surveillance pipelines to improve early-warning accuracy.
papers.Tags: Bayesian,Reaction-Diffusion,EpidemicThreshold,InverseProblems,ParameterUncertainty
papers.Hook: Early prevalence data can determine epidemic thresholds despite unknown individual transmission and recovery rates.

papers.Title: A Theory of Policy Optimization in Post-Training: Coverage Collapse and Reference Resets
papers.Abstract: Policy optimization is central to language model post-training, yet principled guidance remains limited. We revisit its theoretical foundations to identify algorithms that learn near-optimal policies using total samples and gradient steps governed by the base model's response coverage, a measure of how readily it generates optimal responses. We call such algorithms coverage-preserving. This guarantee captures the goal of amplifying capabilities accessible through sampling from the base model.   (1) Coverage collapse. REINFORCE, the basis for PPO and GRPO, can drive the probability of optimal responses to near zero, even as reward improves. This coverage collapse stalls optimization, and convergence can require exponentially many steps despite good initial coverage. The failure arises even with exact gradients and persists under KL regularization to the base model.   (2) Reference resets. We show that repeatedly resetting the KL reference to the most recent policy mitigates coverage collapse. We formalize this intervention in Approximate Policy Mirror Descent (APMD), a meta-algorithm that approximately solves a sequence of KL-regularized RL subproblems. APMD enables stronger regularization, making each subproblem easier to solve, while reference resets allow convergence to global optimality.   (3) Coverage-preserving algorithms. For softmax linear policies over pretrained features, we use APMD to establish the first global convergence guarantees showing that widely used families of post-training algorithms are coverage-preserving. These include stylized PPO and GRPO variants with explicit KL regularization and reference resets, and squared-loss algorithms that implement them implicitly, including those used to train the Kimi models.   These results clarify how regularization, clipping, and objective choice affect the sampling and optimization costs of post-training.
papers.Core_Innovation: Frames policy optimization through the lens of response coverage. It proves REINFORCE-style algorithms can collapse coverage despite reward gains and shows resetting KL reference to the latest policy prevents it.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Artificial Intelligence, Reinforcement Learning, Generative AI
papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund teams immediately implementing reference-reset KL annealing in post-training pipelines. Phase out REINFORCE variants without coverage-preserving mechanisms within six months.
papers.Tags: Policy Optimization, Coverage Collapse, Reference Resets, Post-Training, REINFORCE
papers.Hook: Reference resets prevent coverage collapse, enabling stable post-training policy optimization.

papers.Title: Guiding Data Allocation for Robust Subpopulation Generalization
papers.Abstract: Machine learning models often achieve high average accuracy in the training data while performing poorly on test data due to subpopulation shift. A common data-centric solution is to enforce balanced subgroup proportions, but full balance can be costly, infeasible, and not always necessary. In this work, we study whether balanced training data is the unique optimal configuration for robust subpopulation generalization. We extend a Gaussian feature-model framework to theoretically characterize the performance landscape across general training subgroup distributions. We show that multiple configurations, including substantially imbalanced ones, can perform comparably to the balanced one. We further derive gradient-based directions for adjusting subgroup proportions to improve adjusted accuracy and worst-group accuracy more efficiently. These findings suggest that strategically allocating data offers a more flexible and principled path to robust performance than simple balancing. The code is available at https://github.com/zhaoyingpan/subpop-data-allocation.
papers.Core_Innovation: Extends a Gaussian feature-model framework to characterize performance across arbitrary subgroup distributions, proving balanced data is not uniquely optimal and deriving gradient-based adjustment directions for improved worst-group accuracy
papers.Decision_Perspective: Product teams should fund pilot studies testing gradient-based data allocation within 6 months to validate worst-group accuracy gains. Competitors relying on forced balanced datasets should reassess allocation strategies.
papers.Tags: Subpopulation Generalization,Data Allocation,Gradient-Based Optimization
papers.Hook: Imbalanced data allocation can match balanced performance with targeted gradient adjustments

papers.Title: Kolmogorov-Chapman Maps: Trajectory-Free Learning for Simulating Molecular Dynamics
papers.Abstract: Stochastic differential equations (SDEs) describe stochastic processes across a wide range of scientific domains, including physics, biology, and finance. Although individual numerical integration steps are inexpensive, observing meaningful events or transitions can require millions of sequential steps, resulting in substantial wall-clock simulation time and poor hardware utilization. Deep learning offers an alternative by amortizing many integration steps into a single neural network forward pass, potentially enabling much faster simulation. However, existing supervised approaches typically require long simulated trajectory data, which restricts their applicability. In this work, we introduce Kolmogorov-Chapman Maps (KC-Maps), a method for learning the transition kernel of an SDE that relies only on the trajectory-free marginal samples together with the known drift and diffusion coefficients. Given an initial time and state of a process, KC-Maps models its distribution integrated to any given time, corresponding to the weak solution of the SDE. To recover the correct dynamics, KC-Maps satisfies two key properties: (i) it satisfies the boundary conditions, which we incorporate directly into the neural network architecture, and (ii) it respects the Kolmogorov--Chapman equation, which provides an efficient training objective. We empirically demonstrate that KC-Maps learns to integrate the dynamics of peptide molecular systems and outperforms classical molecular dynamics in terms of GPU-hours.
papers.Core_Innovation: Learns SDE transition kernels from marginal samples alone, eliminating dependency on long simulated trajectories by using known drift and diffusion coefficients
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate R&D budget to prototype KC-Maps integration with molecular dynamics pipelines within 3 months. Redirect computational resources from trajectory-heavy solvers to neural kernel approximation once marginal sample benchmarks confirm speedup.
papers.Tags: SDEs,trajectory-free,molecular dynamics,deep learning
papers.Hook: Trajectory-free SDE learning enables fast simulation from marginal samples only

papers.Title: Adaptive Quantization Preserves Fast Rates for TD Learning over Rate-Limited Channels
papers.Abstract: Motivated by reinforcement learning subject to communication constraints, we study a policy evaluation problem with linear function approximation over a rate-limited channel. In our setup, an agent interacting with an unknown environment (modeled as a Markov Decision Process) transmits quantized estimates of a temporal-difference (TD) learning update direction to a server over a finite-capacity channel. Our goal is to investigate to what extent one can preserve the statistical convergence rates achievable when the channel has infinite capacity. To that end, we propose a new algorithm called Batched Adaptively Quantized TD (BAQ-TD), which uses batching to reduce the variance of the transmitted information, and adaptive quantization to encode innovations. We prove a high-probability finite-time error bound for BAQ-TD, and show that, above a certain finite channel capacity, BAQ-TD preserves the convergence rate of unquantized TD up to logarithmic factors.
